name: Nucleophilic Substitution Unimolecular (SN1)
mechanism: Two-step: 1) Rate-determining ionization → carbocation + leaving group (slow, unimolecular); 2) Nucleophile attacks planar carbocation from either face (fast).
substrate: Tertiary >> secondary > primary (methyl: never). Stability: 3° > 2° > 1°; resonance-stabilized (allylic, benzylic) also favored; carbocation rearrangements (hydride/methyl shift) common to give more stable cation.
nucleophile: Weak nucleophile OK (H2O, ROH). Strong Nu favors SN2/E2 instead.
leavingGroup: Good LG required: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ >> F⁻; -OTs, -OTf excellent. Weak bases are good leaving groups.
solvent: Polar protic (H2O, ROH, HCOOH) stabilizes carbocation via solvation; polar protic accelerates SN1.
stereochemistry: Racemization (with slight inversion excess if ion pair). Planar carbocation attacked from both faces → racemic mixture if starting chiral.
competition: Competes with E1. Heat + weak base favors E1; low T + good Nu favors SN1.
examples: (CH3)3C-Br + H2O → (CH3)3C-OH + HBr (tert-butyl bromide hydrolysis, rate-limiting carbocation)
(CH3)2CH-CH(Cl)-CH3 + CH3OH → ether + HCl (via carbocation, rearrangement possible)
Ph-CH(Cl)-CH3 + H2O → Ph-CH(OH)-CH3 (benzylic SN1, resonance stabilized)
energyDiagram: Two transition states: TS1 (ionization, highest) then carbocation intermediate valley, then TS2 (nucleophilic capture). ΔG‡ dominated by first step.

name: Nucleophilic Substitution Bimolecular (SN2)
mechanism: One-step concerted: nucleophile attacks carbon from backside (180° to leaving group) as LG leaves simultaneously. Transition state: pentacoordinate, trigonal bipyramidal, partial bonds to Nu and LG.
substrate: Methyl > primary > secondary >> tertiary (no SN2). Unhindered backside required. Neopentyl extremely slow.
nucleophile: Strong nucleophile, good polarizability: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ (in protic) reverse in aprotic; RS⁻ > RO⁻ > N3⁻ > OH⁻; charge & basicity increase rate.
leavingGroup: Same as SN1: good LG accelerates (I⁻ best).
solvent: Polar aprotic (DMSO, DMF, acetone, MeCN) → solvates cations, leaves Nu naked and highly reactive. Protic solvents H-bond to Nu and slow SN2.
stereochemistry: Walden inversion: complete inversion of configuration at stereocenter (like umbrella flipping). Enantiomer flips R → S.
competition: Competes with E2. Strong bulky base (t-BuOK) favors E2; small strong Nu + primary substrate → SN2; heat favors elimination.
examples: CH3-Br + OH⁻ → CH3-OH + Br⁻ (methyl, classic SN2)
CH3CH2-I + CN⁻ —DMSO→ CH3CH2-CN + I⁻ (nitrile synthesis)
(R)-CH3CH(Cl)CH3 + I⁻ → (S)-CH3CH(I)CH3 + Cl⁻ (inversion)
Na⁺ ⁻O-CH3 + CH3CH2Br → CH3CH2OCH3 + NaBr (Williamson ether: alkoxide + primary halide)
energyDiagram: Single transition state (pentacoordinate) → no intermediate. ΔG‡ involves both Nu and substrate.

name: Elimination Unimolecular (E1)
mechanism: Two-step: 1) Ionization to carbocation (rate-determining, same as SN1); 2) Weak base abstracts β-H (H on carbon adjacent to C⁺) → π bond forms as LG leaves. Two β-H sets possible → major Saytzeff (more substituted alkene) vs minor Hofmann.
substrate: Tertiary > secondary >> primary. Same as SN1: needs stable carbocation; rearrangements possible.
base: Weak base (H2O, ROH, or substrate itself). Strong bulky base would give E2 instead.
stereochemistry: Not stereospecific; Saytzeff product predominates (thermodynamic, more substituted double bond). No anti-periplanar requirement (carbocation planar).
competition: Always competes with SN1 (same carbocation). SN1 favored at low T, weak Nu, good nucleophile present; E1 favored at high T (entropy: 1→2 molecules), weak non-nucleophilic base.
examples: (CH3)3C-Br + H2O —heat→ (CH3)2C=CH2 + HBr + H2O (tert-butanol E1 dehydration is analogous)
(CH3)2C(Br)CH2CH3 —H2O/heat→ CH3C(=CH2)CH2CH3 (Saytzeff) + CH3CH=C(CH3)2 (major, more substituted)
energyDiagram: Like SN1: TS1 (ionization, RDS) → carbocation → TS2 (deprotonation). Carbocation can branch to SN1 or E1.

name: Elimination Bimolecular (E2)
mechanism: One-step concerted: base abstracts β-H while C-H σ electrons form C=C π and LG leaves simultaneously. Requires anti-periplanar geometry: C-H and C-LG dihedral 180° for optimal orbital overlap (σC-H → σ*C-LG). In Newman projection, H and LG anti.
substrate: Tertiary > secondary > primary (but all can do E2 with strong base; primary needs strong bulky base). Regioselectivity: bulky base (t-BuOK) gives Hofmann (less substituted) due to accessing more accessible H; small base (EtONa) gives Saytzeff (more substituted).
base: Strong base essential: OH⁻, RO⁻, t-BuO⁻ (bulky → Hofmann), DBU, DBN. Strength ↑ → E2 rate ↑.
leavingGroup: Good LG (I, Br, OTs). F⁻ very poor.
solvent: Polar aprotic helps for anionic base; polar protic OK but less optimal.
stereochemistry: Anti-periplanar mandatory → stereospecific. In cyclohexane, leaving group must be axial and anti to H; determines which alkene forms from diastereomers.
competition: Competes with SN2. SN2 favored: primary substrate + small good Nu + low T + polar aprotic. E2 favored: secondary/tertiary + bulky base + high T + hindered substrate.
examples: CH3CH2Br + KOH (alc) —heat→ CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O
CH3CH(Br)CH3 + CH3ONa → CH3CH=CH2 + NaBr + CH3OH (Saytzeff, one product only)
CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3 + t-BuOK → CH3CH2CH=CH2 (Hofmann, 75%, less substituted due to bulky base) + CH3CH=CHCH3 (Saytzeff, 25%)
Cyclohexane: trans-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane + base → more substituted alkene only if anti-H exists
energyDiagram: Single TS: C-H breaking + C=C forming + C-LG breaking partially. Like SN2, one peak.
quickDecisionTable: Primary + strong Nu/small base → SN2; Primary + bulky strong base + heat → E2; Secondary: strong base → E2, weak Nu → SN1/E1; Tertiary + weak Nu/base → SN1/E1 (heat→E1); Tertiary + strong base → E2

name: Electrophilic Addition to Alkenes/Alkynes
mechanism: π bond attacks electrophile (E⁺) → carbocation (or cyclic halonium/mercurinium) intermediate → nucleophile captures. Regiochemistry by carbocation stability (Markovnikov: H/E⁺ adds to carbon with more H to give more stable carbocation on other carbon). Stereochemistry: halonium → anti addition.

variants.name: Hydrohalogenation
variants.regio: Markovnikov (H to C with more H, X to more substituted C)
variants.stereo: via planar carbocation → racemic if chiral center formed

variants.name: Oxymercuration-demercuration
variants.stereo: anti via mercurinium ion; no rearrangement (not true carbocation)

variants.name: Hydroboration-oxidation
variants.regio: Anti-Markovnikov (BH2 to more substituted C, H to less substituted), then OH replaces BH2

variants.name: Halogenation
variants.stereo: Anti addition via cyclic bromonium → trans-diaxial product

variants.name: Halohydrin formation
variants.regio: Br to less substituted C (bromonium opening at more substituted by H2O)

alkyneNotes: Alkyne can add 1 equiv then second equiv: HC≡CH + 2 HBr → CH3CHBr2 (Markovnikov twice, via vinyl cation). Hg²⁺-catalyzed hydration → enol → ketone (Markovnikov: terminal alkyne → methyl ketone).
examples: CH3C≡CH + HBr (1 equiv) → CH3CBr=CH2; + excess HBr → CH3CBr2CH3
CH3C≡CH + H2O —HgSO4/H2SO4→ CH3COCH3 (acetone via enol)

name: Nucleophilic Addition to Carbonyl (C=O)
mechanism: Nucleophile attacks electrophilic carbonyl carbon (δ⁺) → tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate → protonation → alcohol (or addition product). Carbonyl π* is LUMO. No leaving group in aldehyde/ketone; in carboxylic derivatives, tetrahedral intermediate collapses expelling LG → substitution.
reactivityOrder: Aldehyde > ketone > ester > amide (resonance donation reduces electrophilicity). Acyl chloride > anhydride > ester > amide.

variants.name: Grignard addition
variants.products: HCHO + RMgX → RCH2OH (1°); RCHO + RMgX → R2CHOH (2°); RCOR + RMgX → R3COH (3°)

variants.name: Cyanohydrin
variants.notes: Reversible; base-catalyzed; creates new C-C bond + stereocenter

variants.name: Hydride reduction
variants.reagents: NaBH4 (mild, aldehyde/ketone) or LiAlH4 (stronger: acid/ester too)
variants.notes: NaBH4 selective; LiAlH4 requires dry ether, workup

variants.name: Acetal formation
variants.steps: C=O + ROH → hemiacetal → +ROH → acetal + H2O (acid-catalyzed, reversible). Protecting group for carbonyl.

name: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS)
mechanism: Two-step: 1) Electrophile (E⁺) attacks π system → resonance-stabilized σ-complex (arenium ion, carbocation at 3 positions, loss of aromaticity, RDS); 2) Base abstracts H from sp³ carbon → restores aromaticity (fast, exothermic). Overall: C6H5-H + E⁺ → C6H5-E + H⁺.

electrophiles.limitations: Carbocation rearrangement; over-alkylation (product more activating); fails with deactivating ring or -NH2 (complexes AlCl3); primary R⁺ rearranges

electrophiles.advantages: No rearrangement (acylium resonance stable); no over-acylation (product deactivating -COR)

weaklyDeactivatingOrthoPara: -F, -Cl, -Br, -I (halogens: deactivating by -I but o/p by +M lone pair donation)
substituentEffects.notes: Activating = rate ↑ vs benzene; deactivating = rate ↓. o/p directors donate e⁻ ortho/para via resonance; meta directors withdraw; halogens special case.

examples: C6H5CH3 (toluene) + Br2/FeBr3 → o- and p-bromotoluene (alkyl activates o/p, ~60% ortho, 35% para)
C6H5NO2 + Br2/FeBr3 → m-bromonitrobenzene (NO2 deactivates meta)
Phenol + Br2 (H2O, no catalyst) → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white ppt, ultra-activated)
quickTests: Benzene resists Br2 without catalyst (vs alkene instant decolor). Phenol gives white ppt with Br2(aq). Aniline activates strongly but AlCl3 coords to NH2 in Friedel-Crafts, deactivating.

name: Free-Radical Substitution (Alkanes)
mechanism: Chain reaction: Initiation: X2 —hv/Δ→ 2 X· (homolysis). Propagation: X· + R-H → HX + R· (H abstraction); R· + X2 → R-X + X· (regenerates X·). Termination: R·+R·, R·+X·, X·+X· → stable bonds.
selectivity: Reactivity 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl due to radical stability (hyperconjugation, 3° most stable). Cl· is less selective (5:4:1 for 3°:2°:1° at 25°C); Br· highly selective (1600:80:1) → useful for selective bromination at tertiary position (NBS is even more selective for allylic/benzylic).
examples: CH4 + Cl2 —hv→ CH3Cl + HCl; further → CH2Cl2 → CHCl3 → CCl4
CH3CH2CH3 + Br2 —hv→ CH3CHBrCH3 major (secondary radical more stable)
Allylic: CH3CH=CHCH3 + NBS —hv→ CH2BrCH=CHCH3 (resonance allylic radical)
